note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Apply the describe, reflect, take action cycle

evidence.title: ERA cycle reflection on a first lab session
evidence.example: You write a short reflection on a recent learning task using the ERA cycle (Jasper 2013): experience, reflection, action. You describe what happened, reflect on why it went as it did and how you felt, and end with one action you will take next time (for example, after your first practical in a foundation year biology lab, when your results did not match the expected pattern).
evidence.artefact: A one-page reflective entry with three labelled sections, describe, reflect and take action, with tutor feedback on it.
grounding: model: ERA cycle (Jasper 2013)

evidence.title: Structured account of a customer complaint at work
evidence.example: You use the describe, reflect, take action cycle on an event from a part-time job or volunteering (for example, handling a customer complaint during a busy weekend shift in a cafe). You write what happened, think through why it unfolded that way, set one practical action, then try it on a later shift, showing you can apply the cycle to real experience.
evidence.artefact: A short structured reflective account of the work event, ending in an action, with a note on how the action went.
grounding: professional: Writes a structured reflective account of a practice event, ending in actions.
professional: NMC revalidation: written reflective accounts

evidence.title: Balanced evaluation table for a history presentation
evidence.example: You reflect on a piece of assessed work using the evaluation stage of Gibbs' reflective cycle (Gibbs 1988), which asks what was good and what was bad about the experience. You set out strengths first, then weaknesses, each backed by a feedback comment, so the reflection is neither wholly positive nor wholly negative (for example, a first-year history presentation where your research was praised but you ran over time).
evidence.artefact: A two-column evaluation table of strengths and weaknesses, each linked to a specific feedback comment, with a short balanced summary.
grounding: model: Gibbs' reflective cycle, evaluation stage (Gibbs 1988)

evidence.title: Fair review of a coaching session you led
evidence.example: After a real performance, you review what you did fairly and consider other ways you could have worked (for example, a sport coaching student reviewing a session run for an under-12s football club, noting that the warm-up engaged the group well but drill instructions were too long). You record both sides honestly and suggest one alternative approach for next time.
evidence.artefact: A session review sheet with balanced strengths and areas to develop, signed by the club's lead coach.
grounding: professional: Reviews own practice critically and fairly, and considers other ways of working.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

capabilities.statement: Notice what went well and what didn't in your own work

evidence.title: Paired in-action and on-action notes from one task
evidence.example: You keep notes during and after a task, using Schön's (1983) distinction between reflection-in-action, thinking while you are doing something, and reflection-on-action, looking back afterwards. You jot down moments where you noticed something going well or badly as it happened, then compare them with what you notice later (for example, a computing pair-programming session where you spotted a bug early but lost time on testing).
evidence.artefact: Paired notes from one task: in-the-moment jottings and a later reflection-on-action entry, with the differences highlighted.
grounding: model: Reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action (Schön 1983)

evidence.title: Session log from school reading volunteering
evidence.example: In a volunteering role, you note after each session what went well and what did not in your own contribution (for example, as a reading volunteer in a primary school, noticing that a child engaged more when you let them choose the book, but lost focus when you corrected every word). Over several sessions you spot patterns in your own work, not only in the child's.
evidence.artefact: A dated log of five or more volunteering sessions, each noting one thing that went well and one that did not.
grounding: practice: school reading volunteer scheme

evidence.title: Reflective entry rewritten from descriptive to critical
evidence.example: You take an earlier reflective entry and rewrite it using Hatton and Smith's (1995) four types of reflective writing: descriptive writing, descriptive reflection, dialogic reflection and critical reflection. You label the type each paragraph shows, then revise the descriptive passages so they question your reasons, weigh other explanations and consider the wider context (for example, a social work student's entry on a shadowed home visit that recounted events but never asked why the family seemed wary).
evidence.artefact: Original and revised reflective entries, with each paragraph labelled by type and a note on what changed between them.
grounding: model: Four types of reflective writing (Hatton and Smith 1995)

evidence.title: Critical placement reflection discussed with a practice educator
evidence.example: You reflect critically on your practice in a real setting, asking why you acted as you did and what else you could have done (for example, a diagnostic radiography student on placement who rushed a patient's positioning, and reflects on time pressure, communication and the alternatives). You move beyond recounting the event to judging it against the standards expected of you.
evidence.artefact: A placement reflective account discussed with your practice educator, with their written comments on the depth of reflection.
grounding: professional: Reflects critically on own practice and considers alternative approaches.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect critically and consider alternative approaches

capabilities.statement: Turn reflection into a dated action plan

evidence.title: SMART action plan drawn from a reflection
evidence.example: You turn a reflection into an action plan using SMART objectives (Doran 1981): specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. You rewrite vague intentions such as managing time better into dated actions, and justify why each one follows from what the reflection found (for example, an engineering student planning to book two lab slots by set dates before a design report deadline).
evidence.artefact: An action plan table of dated SMART actions, each linked to a line in the reflection, with a review column.
grounding: model: SMART objectives (Doran 1981)

evidence.title: Dated development targets after a mentor observation
evidence.example: You turn reflection from a placement into a dated development plan that someone else reviews (for example, a trainee teacher on school placement who, after a mentor observation, sets dated targets on questioning and classroom routines for the next four weeks). You choose which targets matter most and explain why, then record progress at each review date.
evidence.artefact: The dated development plan with progress notes, initialled by your school mentor at each review.
grounding: professional: Plans and records development actions from reflection on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.6

capabilities.statement: Reflect on motivation and amend strategies that aren't working

evidence.title: Self-regulation review of a failing revision strategy
evidence.example: You analyse a study strategy that is not working using Zimmerman's (2002) cyclical model of self-regulated learning, with its forethought, performance and self-reflection phases. You track your motivation and results over a few weeks, find where the cycle breaks down, and change the strategy, justifying the change with your own evidence (for example, a mathematics student who swaps rereading lecture notes for timed problem sheets after weak tutorial scores).
evidence.artefact: A strategy review with several weeks of tracking data, your analysis by phase, and the amended plan with its results.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)

evidence.title: Changing a work routine after supervision feedback
evidence.example: You use feedback or supervision in a real role to find out what is not working and change how you work (for example, a psychology student employed as a research assistant who learns in supervision that data entry errors come from rushing late in the day, and moves checking to the morning). You reflect on what was driving your motivation and record whether the change worked.
evidence.artefact: Supervision notes or feedback, your follow-up reflection, and a record showing the effect of the changed approach.
grounding: professional: Uses feedback and supervision to find learning needs and change how one works.
professional: Vitae RDF B1 Personal qualities: self-reflection

capabilities.statement: Choose and apply a fuller model (Gibbs, Kolb, Johns)

evidence.title: Assessed reflection with a justified choice of model
evidence.example: You write an assessed reflection after comparing three models: Gibbs' (1988) six-stage reflective cycle, Kolb's (1984) four-stage experiential learning cycle, and Johns' (1995) model of structured reflection, which draws on Carper's ways of knowing. You choose one, justify why it suits this experience, and apply it fully (for example, a midwifery student choosing Johns for an emotionally demanding birth, because its cue questions explore personal and ethical knowing).
evidence.artefact: An assessed reflective essay with a short rationale section comparing the three models and explaining your choice.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-cycle-gibbs-1988
ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984
ing:doc:structured-reflection-johns-1995

evidence.title: Employer reflection template mapped to a named model
evidence.example: You use the reflective model or form your profession or employer expects for a real event, and justify how you applied it (for example, a paramedic science student completing the ambulance service's reflection template after a difficult call, and mapping its prompts to Gibbs' stages). Where the form is fixed, you show how you still reflected in depth within it.
evidence.artefact: A completed reflective template from placement, with a short note mapping its prompts to a named model, reviewed by your mentor.
grounding: professional: Uses the reflective model the profession or employer expects, and justifies the choice.
professional: HCPC standards of proficiency: reflect on and review practice

capabilities.statement: Use reflection for CPD and lifelong learning

evidence.title: Term-long CPD log of linked Kolb cycles
evidence.example: You build a reflective CPD record over a term, using Kolb's (1984) experiential learning cycle to link entries: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation, with each experiment becoming the next experience. You show how repeated cycles add up to development over time rather than one-off reflections (for example, an accountancy student preparing for professional body CPD by tracking growth in client communication).
evidence.artefact: A term-long CPD log of linked cycles, with a summary showing how your practice changed across the entries.
grounding: ing:doc:experiential-learning-kolb-1984

evidence.title: CPD portfolio section mapped to professional standards
evidence.example: You record reflection as CPD evidence in the format a regulator or employer uses (for example, a nursing student writing practice reflective accounts in the style of NMC revalidation, or a graduate teaching assistant mapping reflections to the Advance HE Professional Standards Framework). You select entries that show development, link each to the relevant standard, and discuss them with a peer.
evidence.artefact: A CPD portfolio section with reflective accounts mapped to named standards, and a record of the peer discussion.
grounding: professional: Records reflection on learning and practice as CPD evidence, to a regulator's or employer's standard.
professional: NMC revalidation
professional: Advance HE PSF 2023 A5

capabilities.statement: Reflexivity: how your identity and values shape what you notice

evidence.title: Reflexive commentary using Finlay's variants of reflexivity
evidence.example: You examine how your identity, values and position shape what you notice, using Finlay's (2002) variants of reflexivity: introspection, intersubjective reflection, mutual collaboration, social critique and discursive deconstruction. You choose the variants that fit and show how your background led you to see some things and miss others (for example, a master's student in development studies reflecting on how being an outsider shaped interviews with farmers during fieldwork).
evidence.artefact: A reflexive commentary or methodological appendix naming the variants used, with field note extracts showing their effect.
grounding: ing:doc:variants-of-reflexivity-finlay-2002

evidence.title: Supervision reflection on values shaping a risk judgement
evidence.example: You challenge how your own values affect your practice and the people you work with (for example, a postgraduate social work student realising in supervision that their views about family stability influenced a risk assessment, and asking a colleague to review it). You record what you noticed, what you changed, and how you will keep checking your assumptions in future cases.
evidence.artefact: An anonymised supervision reflection showing the value identified, its effect on your judgement, and the action you took.
grounding: professional: Reflects on own values and challenges their effect on practice.
professional: Social Work England professional standards 4.8
